column2: Achieving goals by satisfying target customers better than alternatives
column3: Identifying a target group's needs before designing an offer illustrates a marketing orientation.
column4: Producing first and assuming customers must accept whatever is made necessarily illustrates customer-oriented marketing.

column2: An orientation stressing availability and production efficiency
column3: A firm focusing mainly on low-cost mass availability follows a different emphasis from researching each segment's needs.
column4: A production orientation necessarily means maximum customisation for every individual customer.

column2: An orientation stressing product quality performance and features
column3: Improving technical features can fail if the product no longer fits customer needs or use conditions.
column4: Superior technical features guarantee market success regardless of customer needs.

column2: An orientation stressing persuasion and sales effort
column3: A selling orientation focuses on pushing an existing offering rather than necessarily starting with target-market needs.
column4: Selling orientation and the marketing concept are identical in their starting point.

column2: Balancing customer satisfaction company goals and long-term social interests
column3: An offer can satisfy immediate wants while still raising long-run environmental or social concerns.
column4: Immediate customer satisfaction automatically proves that all long-term social interests are satisfied.

column2: Perceived benefits relative to the customer's monetary and non-monetary costs
column3: A higher-priced service can offer greater perceived value if reliability and convenience outweigh the extra cost for its target users.
column4: The product with the lowest price always offers the highest value to every customer.

column2: Evaluation of performance relative to expectations
column3: The same performance can satisfy one customer and disappoint another with higher expectations.
column4: Identical performance must create identical satisfaction regardless of expectations.

column2: The coordinated controllable elements used to serve a market
column3: Changing distribution and promotion together can be necessary when launching a product in a new segment.
column4: The marketing mix consists only of advertising and excludes distribution.

column2: Dividing a market into groups with relevant shared characteristics
column3: Grouping customers by different needs can support distinct offers rather than assuming every buyer responds alike.
column4: Segmentation requires assuming identical needs and responses across every buyer.

column2: Grouping customers by location-related characteristics
column3: Adapting a product to regional climate differences uses a geographic segmentation basis.
column4: Grouping customers by climate zone is purely a personality classification.

column2: Grouping customers by measurable population characteristics
column3: Age and income can define demographic segments, although they do not explain every buying motive.
column4: Income categories are psychographic traits rather than demographic variables.

column2: Grouping customers by lifestyles values or personality
column3: Two customers with the same income may belong to different lifestyle segments.
column4: Equal income necessarily implies identical lifestyle and values.

column2: Grouping customers by usage responses or benefits sought
column3: Separating frequent users from occasional users is behavioural segmentation.
column4: Usage frequency is automatically a geographic segmentation variable.

column2: Choosing segments to serve
column3: A small firm can concentrate resources on one attractive segment rather than serving every segment identically.
column4: Targeting requires every firm to serve every segment with exactly the same offer.

column2: Creating a distinctive relevant place in the target customer's perception
column3: Positioning concerns how the target customer understands the offer relative to alternatives.
column4: Positioning means only the physical shelf location of a product.

column2: Serving several selected segments with distinct marketing mixes
column3: Different offers for business travellers and holiday travellers illustrate differentiated targeting.
column4: Offering distinct segment-specific packages is undifferentiated mass marketing.

column2: Focusing on a selected niche or narrow segment
column3: Niche focus can improve specialisation while increasing dependence on that segment.
column4: Concentrating on one niche removes dependence on that niche's demand.

column2: A group of closely related products
column3: Adding another flavour to an existing beverage line can increase line length without adding a new product category.
column4: Adding another beverage flavour necessarily adds a separate unrelated product line.

column2: The number of product lines offered
column3: Adding a cosmetics line to a firm previously selling only beverages increases mix width.
column4: Adding another size within one existing beverage item necessarily increases the number of product lines.

column2: The number of variants within product items or lines as defined
column3: Offering additional sizes of the same shampoo illustrates greater depth rather than necessarily greater width.
column4: Offering more shampoo sizes automatically means entering more unrelated product lines.

column2: Identifying and distinguishing an offer through names symbols and associations
column3: A brand can carry perceived meaning beyond the physical product's features.
column4: A brand is only the legal manufacturing address printed on a package.

column2: Designing the product's container and presentation
column3: Protective packaging and communication can both matter; attractive appearance alone may not prevent transit damage.
column4: Attractive graphics guarantee adequate physical protection in every distribution condition.

column2: The stages of introduction growth maturity and decline as a planning model
column3: Life-cycle stages guide analysis but do not guarantee that every product follows the same duration and path.
column4: Every product must spend exactly the same number of years in each life-cycle stage.

column2: The early market stage after product launch
column3: Low initial sales and high launch costs can produce low or negative profit during introduction.
column4: Every newly launched product must immediately earn maximum profit because it has no sales history.

column2: A stage of expanding adoption and sales
column3: Growing demand can attract competitors, so early sales growth does not guarantee lasting dominance.
column4: Rapid sales growth permanently prevents rival entry.

column2: A stage where market growth slows and competitive pressures intensify
column3: A firm may seek market modification or product improvements rather than assuming maturity means immediate withdrawal.
column4: A product must be withdrawn immediately when its market reaches maturity.

column2: The process of turning ideas into commercially evaluated offerings
column3: Concept testing with prospective buyers precedes or differs from full-scale market commercialisation.
column4: Concept testing requires completing full national commercialisation first.

column2: Estimating commercial feasibility before committing to a product launch
column3: Estimating expected demand costs and profitability differs from merely generating product ideas.
column4: A product idea's novelty alone substitutes for demand and profitability analysis.

column2: A business with high relative market share in a high-growth market
column3: A star may still require substantial investment despite strong relative share.
column4: A star never requires financing because high market share guarantees surplus cash.

column2: A business with high relative share in a low-growth market
column3: A cash cow can help finance other businesses, though the matrix alone does not guarantee every cash-flow result.
column4: A cash cow is defined by low share in a high-growth market.

column2: A business with low relative share in a high-growth market
column3: A question mark requires a strategic decision about investment or exit rather than automatic unlimited funding.
column4: Every question mark must receive unlimited investment regardless of competitive prospects.

column2: Seeking growth with existing products in existing markets
column3: Increasing purchase frequency among current target buyers illustrates market penetration.
column4: Selling an entirely new product in an entirely new market is market penetration.

column2: Taking existing products into new markets
column3: Entering a new region with an existing product illustrates market development rather than product development.
column4: Entering a new region with an unchanged product necessarily means developing a new product.

column2: Entering new markets with new products
column3: Diversification changes both product and market dimensions and may introduce unfamiliar risks.
column4: Diversification retains both the current product and the current market by definition.

column2: Setting price by adding a markup to a specified cost base
column3: A 25% markup on Rs 80 cost gives price Rs 100; that markup differs from a 25% margin on sales.
column4: A 25% markup on Rs 80 cost gives price Rs 106.67 because markup and sales margin are identical.

column2: Pricing guided by customers' perceived value
column3: Different perceived benefits can justify different prices even when production costs are similar.
column4: Value-based pricing requires prices to be determined only by factory cost.

column2: A low initial price intended to build adoption or share
column3: Low introductory pricing is more plausible when price sensitivity and scalable production support the strategy.
column4: A low introductory price guarantees success even when unit cost remains above price indefinitely.

column2: A high introductory price aimed at early high-willingness buyers
column3: An initially high price followed by reductions differs from a low-price entry strategy.
column4: An initially high price followed by reductions is necessarily penetration pricing.

column2: Paid non-personal promotion by an identified sponsor
column3: A paid mass-media advertisement is distinct from an unpaid news report about the organisation.
column4: Any unpaid independent news report is automatically paid advertising.

column2: Direct interaction between a salesperson and prospective buyer
column3: A complex industrial product can benefit from interactive explanation and feedback.
column4: Personal selling provides no opportunity for buyer questions or salesperson adaptation.

column2: Short-term incentives intended to stimulate purchase or trial
column3: A temporary coupon is sales promotion rather than the entire long-term positioning strategy.
column4: A temporary coupon is identical to all of a brand's positioning and product decisions.

column2: Public exposure that is not purchased as controlled advertising space
column3: Independent media coverage may be less controllable than a paid advertisement.
column4: A company always controls the exact wording of independent media coverage just as it controls its paid advertisement.

column2: Promotion directed through channel intermediaries
column3: Incentivising dealers to stock and sell a product illustrates pushing it through the channel.
column4: Dealer incentives alone are a consumer pull strategy by definition.

column2: Promotion aimed at final consumers to stimulate channel demand
column3: Consumer demand generated by brand promotion can encourage retailers to stock the product.
column4: A pull strategy exclusively trains wholesalers and never communicates with final customers.

column2: Intermediaries and arrangements linking producers and users
column3: Using a retailer can expand access while adding coordination and margin considerations.
column4: Adding intermediaries always removes every distribution cost.

column2: Seeking availability through many suitable outlets
column3: A frequently purchased convenience product may benefit from broad outlet availability.
column4: Intensive distribution means granting only one dealer in an entire territory.

column2: Restricting distribution to selected exclusive intermediaries
column3: An exclusive territory can support dealer commitment but may reduce the number of outlets.
column4: Exclusive distribution necessarily maximises the number of competing dealers within the same territory.

column2: Disagreement among distribution participants
column3: A producer selling online below its dealer price can create vertical conflict with dealers.
column4: Producer-dealer conflict is horizontal conflict merely because both sell the same product.

column2: The sequence from need recognition through post-purchase evaluation
column3: Information search and evaluation can precede purchase, while post-purchase experience can influence the next purchase.
column4: The consumer buying process ends permanently at payment and cannot affect repeat decisions.

column2: A participant controlling information or access in organisational purchasing
column3: A receptionist screening supplier access can be a gatekeeper without making the final purchase decision.
column4: Anyone controlling supplier access must automatically be the final purchase decision maker.

column2: A participant shaping specifications or evaluations in organisational purchasing
column3: An engineer can influence technical specifications while another manager authorises the purchase.
column4: Anyone influencing specifications must also personally place and authorise the final order.

column2: Services generally cannot be inspected as physical goods before purchase
column3: A service provider may use credentials or demonstrations to reduce uncertainty about an intangible offering.
column4: Intangibility means customers can never evaluate any evidence about service quality.

column2: Production and consumption of many services occur together
column3: A live consultation can depend on the interaction between provider and client.
column4: Every service can be completely produced and stored independently of all customer interaction.

column2: Unused service capacity generally cannot be inventoried for later sale
column3: An empty seat on a departed flight cannot be sold as that flight's seat tomorrow.
column4: Unused capacity on yesterday's flight automatically becomes extra capacity on tomorrow's flight.

column2: Service performance can vary by provider time and interaction
column3: Training and process design can reduce variability without guaranteeing perfect uniformity.
column4: Service variability makes training and standards completely useless.

column2: Developing sustained mutually valuable customer relationships
column3: Retention can create value through repeat business rather than relying only on one-off acquisition.
column4: Relationship marketing requires ignoring all existing customers and continually replacing them.

column2: Managing customer information and interactions to improve relationships
column3: CRM requires useful processes and suitable data rather than merely purchasing software.
column4: Installing CRM software automatically guarantees loyalty without any service or process change.

column2: Applying marketing to encourage socially beneficial behaviour
column3: A campaign encouraging safe water practices pursues behaviour change rather than necessarily selling a commercial product.
column4: Social marketing is defined solely as paid advertising on social-media websites.

column2: Marketing that considers environmental impacts and claims
column3: Environmental claims should be substantiated; a green label alone does not prove a smaller environmental footprint.
column4: Printing a green symbol automatically proves environmental superiority without evidence.

column2: Communicating directly with selected customers to obtain responses
column3: A targeted catalogue or consented message can seek a measurable direct response without using mass broadcasting.
column4: Direct marketing necessarily requires a television broadcast to the entire population.

column2: Marketing adapted to rural consumers and market conditions
column3: Distribution access purchasing cycles and local needs may require adaptation rather than simply copying an urban plan.
column4: Every rural market has identical demand distribution and language conditions to every urban market.

column2: Coordinating movement storage and related flow of goods
column3: Faster delivery can increase service while raising transport cost, so logistics decisions can involve trade-offs.
column4: The fastest transport option always has the lowest total logistics cost in every situation.
